episodes.title: A New Normal, From Wall Street to Y’all Street, and “Net” Bets 10/5/26
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
US 10-year Treasury yields hit 5.33-5.34%, a 24-year high, as ISM services data showed hot prices-paid alongside last week's hot manufacturing print. Separately, Brazil's EWZ ETF posted its best day since March 2020 (+13%, +36% YTD) after right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed Lula in the first round, pushing the election to an October 25 runoff — both developments carry direct read-through for EM rates and LATAM FX.

**Key points**
- 10yr yield at 5.33-5.34%, 30yr near 5.7%; guests argue this may be a "new normal" tied to nominal GDP trending near 5%, not a recession signal.
- Inflation pressure attributed to three transitory drivers (Russia-Ukraine/"Rand War", chip shortage, tariffs) expected to roll off into next year; AI capex seen as rate-insensitive, dampening policy transmission.
- Watch consumer spending, housing, and credit spreads for early signs tightening is biting.
- Brazil: Bolsonaro (son of jailed former president) beat Lula in round one; HSBC says Brazilian equities can extend gains on a Bolsonaro win; market pricing in his victory; Washington seen as welcoming the outcome, with Beijing having invested heavily in Brazil's energy sector.
- Texas Stock Exchange landed its first primary listing (Energy Transfer, Sonoco, USA Compression, Dillard's) — structural, not immediate FX driver.

**FX / rates implications**
- Higher-for-longer UST yields and a hawkish-but-measured Fed path support USD strength broadly, a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades; watch DXY and front-end EM rates for repricing.
- BRL/EWZ rallying hard on Bolsonaro's market-friendly, pro-US positioning; a runoff win would likely extend Brazil's outperformance vs. EM peers and could reinforce a US-aligned (vs. China-aligned) policy tilt.
- Oil near $90 factored into equity/rates outlook; any Iran de-escalation could lower oil and ease inflation/yield pressure, a tailwind for EM disinflation trades.

**Watch list**
- Brazil runoff: October 25, 2026.
- UST 10yr trajectory beyond 5.33-5.34%; credit spread widening as a tightening-impact signal.
- Iran situation (US B-1 bombers withdrawn from RAF Fairford) — any escalation/de-escalation feeds oil and risk sentiment.

episodes.title: The Credit Market Lens: An Oil Shock (Mostly) Like No Other
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
PIMCO's Credit Market Lens examines why this year's Iran-driven oil shock (seven months in) has not followed the historical playbook: energy prices are up sharply but risk assets, especially IG credit spreads, have barely moved, while Treasury yields rose more than typical growth-scare episodes would suggest. This matters to macro traders because it reframes how commodity shocks transmit to broader risk and rates relative to 2022 or 1991 analogs.

**Key points**
- 6-month WTI contract is roughly 25% higher than end-February, consistent with historical geopolitical oil-shock trajectories.
- IG credit spreads are effectively flat versus February levels; US Treasury yields have moved markedly higher in 2026, tracking the 2022 Russia-Ukraine pattern rather than the 1991 Gulf War pattern.
- Resilience attributed to two structural factors: declining US oil intensity of GDP (half the oil use per unit of GDP versus 1991) and the AI investment cycle, with hyperscaler capex forecast to surpass $1 trillion in 2027.
- Gulf oil exports have recovered to an estimated 80-90% of pre-conflict levels despite Strait of Hormuz disruption risk; US rig counts up 10% this year to ~600, though E&P firms are expanding cautiously.
- Baseline view: energy prices could gradually decline in line with futures curves, but refining/product bottlenecks (diesel, jet fuel, gasoline) remain a transmission risk distinct from crude itself.

**FX / rates implications**
- Higher-for-longer UST yields on inflation-scare repricing are a headwind for EM carry trades and could keep USD supported, pressuring high-beta EM Asia and LATAM FX if the pattern persists.
- Resilient US growth/credit spreads reduce near-term global risk-off tail risk for EM, but a renewed crude or refined-product supply disruption would reintroduce a stagflationary growth-inflation mix unfriendly to EM assets broadly.
- Oil-importing EM currencies (INR, PHP) remain more exposed to sustained energy cost pressure than this credit-market resilience narrative implies.

**Watch list**
- Strait of Hormuz transit flows and Gulf export levels relative to 2025 averages.
- Refining/product market bottlenecks (diesel, jet fuel, gasoline) as a secondary transmission channel.
- US rig count and E&P capex response (Baker Hughes data) for supply-side normalization signals.
